statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether drinking at a young age causes alcohol problems in adulthood, or whether the same family, genetic and personal factors lead to both. In general-population cohorts that recorded the age of the first drink during adolescence, an earlier first drink went with more adult drinking or alcohol problems in some analyses and not in others, and the association often shrank when other risk factors were taken into account. A systematic review found only four such cohorts up to January 2013 (two in the USA and two in Norway; 447 to 1,311 people each; five reports; no meta-analysis; confidence in the review rated critically low on its study card): in an Oslo school cohort, a later first drink went with less drinking and fewer problems at 18 to 21, with control only for parents' and peers' influence; in a US community cohort, a first drink before 11 went with problem drinking by 31 (odds ratios 2.39 and 5.75, depending on where the first drink happened, against a first drink at 11 or later at a family gathering) but not after adjustment for further risk factors, while feeling drunk at the first drink remained a predictor; in the Young in Norway cohort, drinking by 13 to 14, compared with a later first drink, went with frequent intoxication (odds ratio 1.5, 95% CI 1.2 to 1.9) and with an AUDIT score of 8 or more, a screen for risky drinking (1.6, 1.3 to 2.1), at 26 to 27, adjusted for gender, both falling to 1.2 (0.9 to 1.6) when conduct problems in adolescence were also taken into account; in a Seattle cohort of people who started drinking before 21, the age of the first drink was not associated with adult alcohol misuse or with alcohol dependence at any follow-up, but, compared with a first drink at 11 to 14, a first drink before 11 went with a past-year dependence diagnosis at more of the interviews held every 3 years from 21 to 33 (odds ratio 1.68) and, in a later report, with more chronic dependence, essentially unchanged across four adjusted models. The review's abstract says that rigorous adjustment markedly weakens or removes such associations, which its own Seattle summary contradicts; the authors conclude that it is not yet known whether starting earlier leads to adult problems, and found that feeling drunk at the first drink and the start of regular drinking went with adult problems more strongly than the age of the first drink (Maimaris & McCambridge, 2014). In a Minnesota cohort of twins born 1977 to 1984 (1,512 twins at about age 11; drinking reported at the assessment planned for age 14, held at a mean age of 14.8; outcomes at about 25), twins who had drunk without their parents' permission by that assessment already differed beforehand from twins who had not, notably in delinquent behaviour and in their parents' drinking and smoking; after weighting for 29 characteristics of the twins and their families measured at about 11, early drinking was associated with a higher adult alcohol-use score (standardized coefficient 0.57, SE 0.06), and within twin pairs who differed in early drinking the association was a little over a third as large but remained (0.21, SE 0.09, in all pairs; 0.22, SE 0.10, in identical pairs, who share all their genes and their family; the estimates for identical and fraternal pairs did not differ significantly), whereas within identical pairs early drinking was not clearly associated with symptoms of alcohol abuse or dependence (0.17, SE 0.14) (Irons et al., 2015). Twin comparisons remove what co-twins share, not differences between them such as their own early use of tobacco or other drugs. Grant & Dawson (1998), the national survey analysis of age at first drug use and drug use disorders, is not yet read. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
plain: Does drinking young lead to alcohol problems later? This is not known. In the few studies that followed young people over time, in the US and Norway, drinking early went with more drinking problems as an adult in some studies, but in others the link went away once other risks, such as behaviour problems in adolescence, were taken into account. Feeling drunk at the first drink and starting to drink regularly went with later problems more strongly than the age of the first drink. In US twins, the twin who had drunk without their parents' permission by about age 15 drank more as an adult than the twin who had not, even in identical twins, though the difference was smaller than when all the young people in the study were compared; in identical twins, early drinking was not clearly linked to later symptoms of an alcohol disorder. Twin studies cannot rule out other differences between twins, such as smoking or other drug use. See the contested question.
population: Young people in general-population cohorts followed from adolescence into adulthood: four cohorts in the USA and Norway in a systematic review (447 to 1,311 people each) and Minnesota twins born 1977–1984 (1,512 at about age 11)
exposure: An earlier first drink (more than a few sips; definitions differed, from before 11 to by 13–14), recorded in adolescence; in the twin study, drinking without parental permission, or being intoxicated, by the assessment planned for age 14 (mean age 14.8)
comparator: People who started drinking later (in the Rutgers cohort, a first drink at 11 or later at a family gathering; in the Seattle cohort, a first drink at 11 to 14); in the twin study, twins who had not, including their own co-twin
outcome: Adult drinking, alcohol problems and alcohol dependence (consumption indices, problem scales, AUDIT, DSM-IV symptom counts or diagnoses, at 18 to about 33)
magnitude: Not estimable as a causal effect. Maimaris & McCambridge (2014), four cohorts, no pooling: Oslo (n = 522) structural coefficients −3.465 for debut age on consumption and −13.828 on a problem index (p < 0.0001), with parental and peer control only; Rutgers (n = 447, people with data at every wave) first drink before 11, OR 2.39 (95% CI 1.10–5.20) at a family gathering and 5.75 (1.53–21.54) elsewhere, both against a first drink at 11 or older at a family gathering, for lifetime problem drinking by 31, not significant in the fully adjusted model (coefficient −0.0631), feeling drunk at the first drink 0.3848 (p < 0.0001); Seattle (n = 808 who started drinking before 21), against a first drink at 11–14, for a first drink before 11, at 15–17 and at 18–20: misuse at any follow-up ORs 0.96, 1.40 and 0.64, dependence at any follow-up 1.49, 1.16 and 0.35 (all p > 0.05); first drink before 11 and the number of interviews (every 3 years from 21 to 33) with a past-year dependence diagnosis OR 1.68 (p < 0.05; no intervals), later report (n = 706) chronicity β 0.44 unadjusted and 0.45 to 0.53 in four adjusted models; Young in Norway (n = 1,311), drinking by 13–14 against later, adjusted for gender: frequent intoxication OR 1.5 (1.2–1.9) and AUDIT 8 or more 1.6 (1.3–2.1); both 1.2 (0.9–1.6) with conduct problems added. Irons et al. (2015), drinking without parental permission by the age-14 assessment (mean age 14.8), standardized β (SE): adult alcohol-use index, weighted 0.57 (0.06), within all discordant pairs 0.21 (0.09), identical pairs 0.22 (0.10), fraternal pairs 0.20 (0.14) (within-pair estimates 0.37 and 0.39 of the weighted one, editors' calculation; zygosity did not significantly moderate any within-pair effect); alcohol abuse or dependence symptoms, weighted 0.36, all pairs 0.24 (0.11), identical 0.17 (0.14), fraternal 0.34 (0.16); intoxication by the age-14 assessment and alcohol abuse or dependence symptoms within all pairs 0.29 (0.15). The twin study's printed p-values are not used (card reporting issue).

risk_of_bias.note: The cohorts adjusted for different, incomplete sets of confounders (only one for family history; none for genetic liability), some possibly on the causal path; confidence in the review is critically low (card sc_maimaris_2014: AMSTAR 2, no protocol, no list of excluded studies, single-reviewer screening); in the twin study, confounders not shared by co-twins, such as their own early tobacco or drug use, were not measured, and 12% were not seen at about 25 (card sc_irons_2015: ROBINS-E, some concerns).

inconsistency.note: The association survived adjustment in some analyses (Seattle chronicity; within twin pairs for adult drinking) and not in others (Rutgers, Young in Norway, Seattle misuse and any dependence; identical pairs for abuse or dependence symptoms).

indirectness.note: Rated as worded: four cohorts in the USA and Norway and one Minnesota twin cohort, with outcomes from drinking scores to symptom counts and chronic dependence, all stated.

imprecision.note: Cohorts of 447 to 1,311 people with small exposure groups (a first drink before 11); no intervals for the Seattle estimates; the identical-pair estimates rest on roughly 97 discordant pairs (editors' estimate on the study card), with standard errors close to the estimates.

publication_bias.note: The review judges publication bias a profound threat but could not test it; not rated down separately, since the certainty is already at its floor.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low; down one each for risk of bias, inconsistency and imprecision: very low, the floor. Counted once: the two Seattle reports share one cohort (four cohorts, not five studies). The twin study's printed p-values are not valid (card reporting issue), so significance is judged from coefficients and standard errors. The claim concerns cause, so its relation is insufficient evidence; the association of an earlier first drink with more adult drinking in several cohorts is reported in it, not rated as a separate claim. Grant & Dawson (1998), on age at first drug use, is not yet read; the alcohol landmark from the same survey (Grant & Dawson, 1997) has no reference record in the library. Status contested: credible analyses point both ways and the review's own authors say the answer is not known, so the six-part debate box applies.

debate.question: Does drinking at a young age cause alcohol problems in adulthood, or do the same family, genetic and personal factors lead both to early drinking and to later problems?
debate.evidence_yes: In the Seattle cohort, a first drink before 11 went with more chronic alcohol dependence to age 33, and the association was essentially unchanged after adding peer, school, behavioural and substance-use factors in four models (β 0.44 unadjusted, 0.45 to 0.53 adjusted), with none of the three alternative explanations tested supported; in the Oslo cohort, a later first drink went with less drinking and fewer problems at 18 to 21 (Maimaris & McCambridge, 2014). In Minnesota twins, drinking without parental permission by the assessment planned for age 14 (mean age 14.8), recorded at that assessment, was associated with a higher adult alcohol-use score after weighting for 29 childhood characteristics (0.57) and within twin pairs who differed in early drinking (0.21), including identical pairs, who share all their genes and their family (0.22, SE 0.10); across all discordant pairs it was also associated with symptoms of alcohol abuse or dependence (0.24, SE 0.11). The authors read the within-pair results as supporting an effect of early drinking, while noting that confounders not shared by co-twins could explain them (Irons et al., 2015).
debate.evidence_no: In two of the four general-population cohorts the association did not survive adjustment: in the Rutgers cohort a first drink before 11 went with problem drinking by 31 (odds ratios 2.39 and 5.75, against a first drink at 11 or later at a family gathering) only before adjustment for further risk factors, and in the Young in Norway cohort drinking by 13 to 14 went with frequent intoxication and risky drinking at 26 to 27 (1.5 and 1.6, adjusted for gender) only until adolescent conduct problems were taken into account (both 1.2, 0.9 to 1.6); in the Seattle cohort the age of the first drink was not associated with adult alcohol misuse or with dependence at any follow-up; the Oslo estimate controlled only for parents' and peers' influence; feeling drunk at the first drink and starting regular drinking went with adult problems more strongly than the age of the first drink; and the review's authors conclude that it is not yet known whether starting earlier leads to adult problems (Maimaris & McCambridge, 2014). In the twin study, twins who drank by the assessment planned for age 14 already differed beforehand in delinquent behaviour and in their parents' drinking and smoking; for the adult alcohol-use score the within-pair association was a little over a third of the weighted one (0.21 against 0.57, ratio 0.37; editors' calculation); and within identical pairs early drinking was not clearly associated with symptoms of alcohol abuse or dependence (0.17, SE 0.14), nor was intoxication by that assessment across all pairs (0.29, SE 0.15) (Irons et al., 2015).
debate.neither_can_show: No randomized evidence exists, since the age of a first drink cannot be assigned at random. The cohorts recorded the first drink in adolescence, which avoids recalling it decades later, but they can adjust only for what they measured: only one adjusted for family history of alcohol problems, none controlled for genetic liability, and adjusting for peers or behaviour that early drinking may itself change can remove part of a real effect. In two of the four cohorts the first drink of late starters was not recorded in adolescence or 3 years before the outcome. Co-twin comparisons remove everything twins share (all genes in identical pairs, half in fraternal pairs, and the family they grew up in) but not what differs between them, such as their own early smoking, other drug use or friends, and random error in reporting early drinking shrinks within-pair estimates on its own; the identical-pair estimates rest on roughly 97 discordant pairs, so a non-significant result there is not evidence of no effect. Both twin exposures were yes-or-no, so nothing is known about how much the young people drank.
debate.editors_reading: Editors' reading (certainty: very low). An earlier first drink goes with more adult drinking in several cohorts, and part of that link reflects differences that were there before the first drink, such as behaviour problems and family drinking: in two of four cohorts the link disappeared after adjustment, and in twins it was a little over a third as large within pairs as in the comparison weighted for childhood characteristics. Within identical twins, early drinking still went with more adult drinking, which leaves room for an effect of early drinking itself, but it was not clearly linked to symptoms of alcohol use disorder, and the twin design cannot exclude differences between co-twins. The evidence read here cannot say whether delaying the first drink would reduce adult alcohol problems; in the review, feeling drunk at the first drink and early regular drinking were more strongly linked to adult problems than the age of the first drink.
debate.what_would_settle_it: Pooled analyses of identical twin pairs who differ in early drinking across several twin registries, large enough to estimate effects on alcohol use disorder precisely, with early drinking recorded repeatedly (age, amount, intoxication) and the twins' own earlier behaviour and substance use measured; harmonized analyses of several large birth or school cohorts with the first drink recorded as it happens and the same confounders; and natural experiments that shift the age of first drinking for reasons unrelated to the person, such as changes in minimum legal drinking ages.

statement: In the samples one review found, a large share of people who use cocaine also used alcohol, and in most samples cannabis, on the same occasions or in the same period, but the share varied widely with the sample and with the definition used. The review combined 16 estimates (11 studies from one PubMed search, January 1990 to June 2017, and 5 of the authors' own analyses of US data sets; 10 from the USA, 3 from Canada, 2 from Brazil and 1 from Denmark; study years 1985 to 2017; samples ranging from household surveys to treatment services, emergency departments, raves and drug courts; all but one by self-report; confidence in the review rated critically low on its study card). Its random-effects averages were 74% (95% CI 50% to 89%) for alcohol and 38% (20% to 60%) for cannabis used on the same occasion as cocaine (the review's definition; the sources asked, for example, about use within a couple of hours, at the first cocaine use, in the same session or to come down from a cocaine high), and 77% (62% to 87%) for alcohol and 64% (47% to 79%) for cannabis used in the same period (from the past 30 days to a lifetime, both positive in one urine test, or an unstated window; where a source gave several windows, the shortest was used), with heterogeneity of 97% to 99% in all four; single sources ranged from about a quarter to nearly all for alcohol and from about 1 in 10 to more than 9 in 10 for cannabis, and the lowest figures came from the narrowest question: in two St Louis samples of women who had used cocaine in the past 30 days, 23.5% and 36.1% said they had used alcohol, and 9.3% and 12.3% cannabis, to come down from cocaine, while 79.5% and 71.3% had drunk alcohol that month. This matters for research on cocaine: of the 40 most recent human brain-imaging studies of cocaine up to January 2018, none excluded people who drink alcohol or use cannabis (two excluded people who had used cannabis in the past week; only 10 excluded alcohol dependence and 10 cannabis dependence, although in most of the studies such dependence was a reason to exclude comparison participants), so unless these drugs were accounted for, their findings may mix effects of cocaine with effects of alcohol or cannabis; of 40 recent animal studies of cocaine, 2 also gave alcohol, both earlier in life (before birth or in adolescence), and none gave cannabis, so those animal studies did not model how people combine these drugs, although the authors note that leaving other drugs out is valid for some questions (Liu et al., 2018). Tobacco, which the authors think may be combined with other drugs, especially alcohol, even more often than cocaine with alcohol, was not counted; the sources were not appraised, the ranges in the text do not all match the review's table, and how many sources entered each average was shown only in a figure that could not be read; an editors' recalculation from the table reproduced two of the four averages (cannabis on the same occasion, alcohol in the same period) but not the other two. What happens in the body when cocaine and alcohol are taken together is in the answer on mixing cocaine and alcohol. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: How often do people who use cocaine also use alcohol or cannabis? Often, in the studies one review found. On average, about 3 in 4 had used alcohol on the same occasion as cocaine or in the same period, and about 4 in 10 had used cannabis on the same occasion, 6 in 10 in the same period. But the numbers varied hugely between groups, from about a quarter to nearly everyone for alcohol and from about 1 in 10 to more than 9 in 10 for cannabis, depending on who was asked and exactly what was asked. This matters for research: none of 40 recent brain-scan studies of cocaine left out people who drink or use cannabis (two left out people who had used cannabis in the past week), so their results may mix up the effects of different drugs, while animal studies almost never gave a second drug. Tobacco was not counted.

statement: In people born from 1950 to 1993 and adopted in Sweden outside their biological family (adoptions by relatives or by a biological parent's partner excluded), with register information on both adoptive parents and at least one biological parent, both what was passed on from their biological parents and features of the adoptive home they grew up in were associated with a later register record of drug problems; the study estimated no heritability percentage. Of 18,115 adoptees followed in national registers to 2009 (a record meant a diagnosis of a drug use disorder or drug psychosis in hospital, outpatient, primary-care or death records; a conviction under two crime-register codes for crimes related to drug abuse, convictions only for alcohol-related crimes or only for drug trafficking or possession not counting; or long-term high-volume collection of prescribed sedatives, hypnotics or opioids; alcohol and tobacco excluded; the study calls this 'drug abuse'), 4.5% had a record, against 2.9% of everyone in Sweden born in the same years. Adoptees whose biological parent had a record, though they were not raised by that parent, had one in 8.6% of cases against 4.2% when neither biological parent had (odds ratio 2.09, 95% CI 1.66 to 2.62), and in 11.9% when both had; records were also shared with biological siblings raised apart (full siblings, odds ratio 1.84, 1.28 to 2.64; half siblings, 1.41, 1.19 to 1.67). In the adoptive home, records were shared with adoptive siblings, who were not biologically related to the adoptee: 6.2% of the adoptive siblings of adoptees with a record had one, against 3.2% of the adoptive siblings of adoptees without (odds ratio 1.95, 1.43 to 2.65), and the adoptive mother's divorce and an adoptive parent's death were also associated with a record; adoptees raised by an adoptive parent with a record had one in 6.8% of cases against 4.5%, an imprecise estimate that included no difference (1.55, 0.86 to 2.80), with only 1.0% of adoptive parents affected. On the scale of absolute risk, an adverse adoptive home added more risk for adoptees whose biological relatives' records put them at higher risk, an interaction the paper does not report on the odds scale; at the lowest level of the biological-relative index the added risk could not be told apart from none (Kendler et al., 2012). An adoption study separates the family that passes on genes from the family that raises a child, but what passes from biological parents includes the pregnancy, care before placement (up to about 3 in 10 adoptees may have joined their adoptive family after age 5, by a census-based estimate) and how agencies matched children to homes (modest, by the authors' judgment), as well as genes. The authors report that children usually spent the time before placement in a nursery or foster home rather than with their biological parents, and that later placement did not go with a higher risk (odds ratio 0.96 per year before adjustment, 1.00 after); their argument against effects in the womb rests on 9.9% with an affected biological father against 8.2% with an affected mother, overlapping intervals without a test. As summarized, without figures, by a narrative review, twin studies find that genes and both shared and individual environment influence whether people start using tobacco, alcohol or cannabis, that genes matter more for regular use and dependence, and that the environment twins share is no longer detectable for regular use or dependence in adulthood though it is in adolescence (the adoptive-sibling association above, if it reflects the shared home, does not fit this summary well); single genetic variants have small effects that replicate poorly, scores combining many variants explained less than 1% of the variation in alcohol dependence, and the size of genetic influence has been reported to differ between environments (Prom-Wormley et al., 2017, second-hand). A heritability, where one is given, describes how much of the differences between people in one population at one time go with differences in their genes; it is not the share of any one person's risk that comes from genes (the editors' explanation; Visscher et al., 2008, on what heritability means, is not yet read). Certainty: low. Status: single study.
plain: Do genes and the home you grow up in shape drug problems? In a large Swedish study of adopted children, both were linked to drug problems. Children whose birth parent had a drug problem in official records had one themselves about twice as often (about 9 in 100, against 4 in 100 when neither birth parent did), even though other parents raised them. Drug problems were also shared within adoptive families, between children not related by birth: when an adopted child had one, about 6 in 100 of their adoptive brothers and sisters did too, against 3 in 100 when the adopted child did not. Divorce or a parent's death in the adoptive family also went with more drug problems. The study did not work out a percentage due to genes, and what comes from birth parents also includes the pregnancy and the time before adoption. A percentage due to genes, where studies give one, describes differences between people in one place and time; it does not say how much of one person's risk comes from genes.
population: People born 1950–1993 and adopted in Sweden outside their biological family (adoptions by relatives or by a biological parent's partner excluded), with register information on both adoptive parents and at least one biological parent, who first lived with their adoptive parents by age 10 by a census-based estimate (18,115 adoptees; national registers to 2009); twin studies summarized without figures by a narrative review
exposure: A register record of drug problems in biological parents or in biological siblings not raised with the adoptee (what passes from biological relatives: genes, pregnancy, care before placement), and in adoptive siblings or parents, or disruption of the adoptive home (the rearing environment)
comparator: Adoptees whose biological, or adoptive, relatives had no such record
outcome: A register record of drug problems (the study's 'drug abuse': drug use disorder or drug psychosis diagnoses; convictions under two crime-register codes for crimes related to drug abuse, with alcohol-only, trafficking and possession convictions excluded; or long-term high-volume collection of prescribed sedatives, hypnotics or opioids; alcohol and tobacco excluded)
magnitude: Kendler et al. (2012): adoptees with a record 4.5% (95% CI 4.2–4.8; 820 people) vs 2.9% nationally for the same birth years. Biological parent with vs without a record 8.6% vs 4.2%, OR 2.09 (1.66–2.62); none, one or both biological parents 4.2%, 8.2%, 11.9%; biological father 9.9% (7.2–12.1), mother 8.2% (6.3–10.5). Biological full siblings raised apart, record in 10.7% of the full siblings of adoptees with a record vs 6.1% of those of adoptees without, OR 1.84 (1.28–2.64); half siblings 7.4% vs 5.3%, OR 1.41 (1.19–1.67). Adoptive siblings of adoptees with vs without a record 6.2% vs 3.2%, OR 1.95 (1.43–2.65); adoptees raised by an adoptive parent with vs without a record 6.8% vs 4.5%, OR 1.55 (0.86–2.80). Multivariable: adoptive mother's divorce OR 1.31 (1.03–1.68), adoptive parent's death 1.37 (1.08–1.73). Interaction on the probability scale 0.0005 per decile × decile (0.0001–0.0008): each decile of the adoptive-home index added about 0.15 percentage points of risk at the lowest decile of the biological-relative index (the main effect with the interaction term, 0.0015, −0.0006 to 0.0036, an interval that includes no added risk) and about 0.6 at the highest (editors' calculation on the study card, recomputed with deciles coded 0 to 9). Later placement: odds ratio 0.96 per year before adjustment, 1.00 after. No heritability estimated. As summarized by Prom-Wormley et al. (2017): polygenic scores explained less than 1% of the variance in alcohol dependence; no twin heritability figure for any drug use disorder is given.

statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether women in general go from first use of alcohol or other drugs to dependence, or to treatment, faster than men (the idea called 'telescoping'): the faster course was described mostly in people in treatment and self-help groups, from ages they recalled years later; the one general-population test read here, for alcohol, did not find the full pattern; and a US general-population survey of cannabis use disorder, not read here, is described as finding a shorter course in women. In two pooled US national household surveys (NLAES, 1991–1992, response 90%, and NESARC, 2001–2002, response 81%; 53,238 US-born adults aged 18 to 57; every age recalled at a single interview), women had their first drink later than men (on average at 19.0 against 17.8 years; the gap narrowed from 3.0 years in people born 1934–1943 to 0.4 years in those born 1974–1983). Among the 38,309 lifetime drinkers (more than 12 drinks ever), men had a higher hazard of alcohol dependence than women in every birth cohort (hazard ratios 1.36 to 1.79, adjusted for survey, race and ethnicity, income, education, urbanicity and age at first drink, and, according to the table's footnote though not the Methods, for age). The authors read these hazards, the survival curves and a significant interaction of cohort, gender and time (its estimates not shown) as men becoming dependent faster, especially in younger cohorts. In the editors' reading, a hazard among all drinkers combines the chance of ever becoming dependent with the speed of getting there, and because the average times below were similar, the higher hazard in men mostly reflects that more men became dependent (in the table's unweighted counts, 23.7% of male and 16.2% of female lifetime drinkers; editors' arithmetic). Among the people who did become dependent, the group whose timing treatment-sample studies measure, the average time from first drink to dependence was about the same in women and men (5.6 against 5.8 years; unadjusted); it was shorter in women born 1964–1973 (3.7 against 4.2 years) and, not marked significant, in those born 1954–1963 (5.5 against 6.4), and longer, not significantly, in women of the other three cohorts. Among people with dependence, men also had a higher hazard of first alcohol treatment, significantly in two of five birth cohorts (1.55 and 1.42) (Keyes et al., 2010). The authors conclude that telescoping is not evident in the general population, although their Discussion's statement that women were faster on neither measure goes further than their own table. As described in a historical critique, the idea goes back to a 1952 WHO committee report and to stage models built from the recalled drinking histories of 98 men in Alcoholics Anonymous, with 15 women's answers set aside; the phrase 'telescoped development' was first used in 1958; the 1989 study usually credited with defining the term asked 33 women and 105 men from treatment programmes and self-help groups to recall four landmark ages, and the interval from first alcohol-related problem to first treatment was 4.3 years shorter on average in the women; 75 of 103 articles citing that study used it as background without testing it; and the critique's authors recommend dropping the term (Marks & Clark, 2018). The same critique describes a US general-population survey (NESARC, by its reference title; 1,217 women and 3,297 men) as finding the time from first cannabis use to cannabis use disorder 2.5 years shorter in women, without giving its timing measure or adjustment (Khan et al., 2013, as described by Marks & Clark, 2018). A narrative review lists faster progression in women for alcohol, cannabis, cocaine (in people in the justice system) and prescription opioids, but not heroin, found mainly in women already in treatment, and, following an earlier review, explains the difference from population surveys by who is sampled: women in treatment likely have more severe disorders (McHugh et al., 2018; its cannabis citation points to a general-population paper on alcohol dependence). The same group's earlier review states as established that women advance faster from use to regular use to first treatment for alcohol, opioid and cannabis dependence, citing six studies, among them treatment samples and one population survey (Dawson, 1996) that the review itself describes elsewhere as showing no earlier treatment entry for women (Greenfield et al., 2007). Randall et al. (1999), a treatment-sample study that the papers read describe in opposite ways, is not yet read. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
plain: Do women go from first use to problems faster than men? This has not been shown for women in general. The idea, called 'telescoping', came mostly from small groups of people in treatment or in Alcoholics Anonymous, who had to remember years later when each step happened, and its stages were first drawn from men's stories. In two big US surveys of adults in the general population, women had their first drink later than men, and fewer women than men became dependent on alcohol. Among the people who did become dependent, women got there about as fast as men, on average about 6 years after their first drink, and a little faster in one age group. The survey's authors read their results as men getting there faster; the editors think this mostly shows that more men became dependent. A US survey about cannabis, known here only from another paper's short description, found a faster course in women. A review suggests that the women who reach treatment may have more severe problems, which would explain why a faster course shows up in treatment. All these studies relied on memory. See the contested question.
population: Adults in two pooled US national household surveys (NLAES 1991–1992 and NESARC 2001–2002; US-born, aged 18 to 57; 53,238 people, 38,309 of whom were lifetime drinkers, with more than 12 drinks ever) for alcohol; for other drugs and for treatment and self-help samples, studies described in a historical critique and two narrative reviews, among them one general-population survey of cannabis use disorder
exposure: Being a woman (the studies compare by gender and do not separate sex from gender)
outcome: Time from first use to dependence and from dependence to first treatment ('telescoping'), every step recalled at one interview or in questionnaires
magnitude: Not estimable as a general difference in speed. General-population surveys, alcohol (Keyes et al., 2010): age at first drink, women 19.0 vs men 17.8 years (gap 3.0 years in people born 1934–1943, 0.4 in those born 1974–1983; editors' subtraction); hazard of dependence among all lifetime drinkers (more than 12 drinks), men vs women, 1.56 (95% CI 1.35–1.79), 1.36 (1.23–1.50), 1.46 (1.33–1.62), 1.79 (1.58–2.02) and 1.71 (1.34–2.20) for people born 1974–1983, 1964–1973, 1954–1963, 1944–1953 and 1934–1943 (a mixture of the chance of dependence and its speed, read by the authors as faster progression in men; whether age was adjusted for is stated inconsistently); share of lifetime drinkers with a time to dependence in the unweighted Table 1 counts, men 23.7% vs women 16.2% (4,631 of 19,549 and 3,121 of 19,263; editors' arithmetic; these counts total 7,752, against 8,564 people with dependence in the hazard analysis); mean time from first drink to dependence among people who became dependent (unadjusted), women 5.6 vs men 5.8 years (ratio 1.04, not significant), born 1964–1973 3.7 vs 4.2 years (p = 0.02), born 1954–1963 5.5 vs 6.4 years (not marked significant; t about 2.4 from the printed means and standard errors, an editors' approximation on the study card), and longer in women in the other three cohorts (3.1 vs 2.8, 8.6 vs 7.9 and 11.8 vs 10.4 years; none marked significant); hazard of first treatment among people with dependence, men vs women, 1.16 (0.77–1.76), 1.55 (1.22–1.96), 1.42 (1.16–1.73), 1.20 (0.91–1.58) and 1.38 (0.84–2.26) in the same cohort order; mean time from dependence to first treatment among people treated, born 1934–1943, women 19.4 vs men 23.5 years (the overall means, 6.1 vs 7.0, cannot be reconciled with the cohort rows and are not used). debate.question: Do women go from first use of alcohol or other drugs to dependence, or to treatment, faster than men, or does the faster course seen in treatment samples come from who reaches treatment and from how the timing was remembered?
debate.evidence_yes: The faster course was described mostly in people in treatment. In the 1989 study usually credited with defining the term, 33 women and 105 men from treatment programmes and self-help groups recalled their landmark ages: the women had started drinking about 2 years later and had first been drunk about 3 years later, entered treatment at the same age, and went from their first alcohol-related problem to their first treatment 4.3 years faster on average; in an earlier Iowa treatment sample (3,132 men and 395 women), women reached treatment about 2 years after a first attempt to quit and men about 3 (as described by Marks & Clark, 2018). A US general-population survey (NESARC, by its reference title; 1,217 women and 3,297 men) is described as finding the time from first cannabis use to cannabis use disorder 2.5 years shorter in women, which is evidence from outside treatment; its timing measure and adjustment are not given and it is not read here (Khan et al., 2013, as described by Marks & Clark, 2018; a narrative review's citation for cannabis points to a different paper). A narrative review lists faster progression in women for alcohol, cannabis, cocaine (in people in the justice system) and prescription opioids (McHugh et al., 2018), and the same group's earlier review states faster progression to first treatment as established for alcohol, opioid and cannabis dependence (Greenfield et al., 2007). In the general-population alcohol surveys, among the people who did become dependent, women born 1964–1973 got there faster than men (on average 3.7 against 4.2 years), the printed figures suggest the same for women born 1954–1963 (5.5 against 6.4 years, not marked significant; an editors' approximation on the study card), and among people who were treated, women born 1934–1943 reached treatment sooner after dependence began (19.4 against 23.5 years) (Keyes et al., 2010).
debate.evidence_no: In the only general-population test read, two pooled US national surveys (1991–1992 and 2001–2002; 53,238 US-born adults aged 18 to 57), women started drinking later than men, but among the lifetime drinkers men had a higher hazard of alcohol dependence in every birth cohort (1.36 to 1.79) and, among people with dependence, a higher hazard of first treatment (significant in two of five cohorts, 1.55 and 1.42), after adjustment for survey, race and ethnicity, income, education, urbanicity and age at first drink (and, by the table's footnote, age); the authors read the dependence hazards as men progressing faster, especially in younger cohorts. Among people who became dependent, the average time from first drink to dependence was about the same in women and men (5.6 against 5.8 years) and, in three of five cohorts, longer in women, not significantly; the authors conclude that telescoping is not evident in the general population (Keyes et al., 2010). A narrative review, following an earlier one, explains the gap between treatment samples and population surveys by who is sampled, since women who reach treatment likely have more severe disorders, and reports that telescoping was not found for heroin (McHugh et al., 2018). The historical critique shows that the stages that define telescoping were drawn from the recalled histories of men in Alcoholics Anonymous (98 men analysed, 15 women's answers set aside), that the 1989 study was small and drawn from treatment and self-help settings, and that 75 of 103 papers citing it used it as background without testing it; it argues that, with women as the reference group, men's longer course might have been called magnification, and recommends discarding the term (Marks & Clark, 2018).
debate.neither_can_show: Every timing in these studies was recalled, often decades later, at a single interview or in a questionnaire; none was recorded as it happened, and no study read tested whether women and men remember timing differently (the surveys' recall check, which the authors read as showing limited recall bias, tested only whether dependence beginning at 25 or later was reported less often by members of the same birth cohorts interviewed 10 years later). Treatment samples time only people who reached treatment, so a group that reaches treatment soon after its problems begin will look fast whatever its course in the population. In the general-population surveys, hazards among all drinkers combine the chance of ever becoming dependent with the speed of getting there, so on their own they cannot say who is faster; the averages among people who became dependent come closer to speed but are unadjusted and depend on age at interview, and the youngest cohort, interviewed only as young adults, could contribute only early steps. People who died before the surveys, or were older than 57, are missing. None of these designs separates sex (biology) from gender (roles, access to treatment, stigma); the general-population evidence read is for alcohol in the USA only, and the cannabis survey is known only from a short description in another paper.
debate.editors_reading: Editors' reading (certainty: very low). The faster course in women was described mostly in small treatment and self-help samples, from recalled ages, and the idea grew out of stage models built from men's recalled histories. In the one general-population test read, for alcohol in the USA, women were less likely than men to become dependent and, once dependent, had a lower hazard of reaching treatment, and those who did become dependent got there about as fast as men on average, faster in one birth cohort; the authors read the same data as men progressing faster, a reading that rests on hazards that mix the chance of dependence with its speed and on an interaction whose estimates are not shown. So the evidence read here does not show that women in general move faster from first use to dependence; whether women who do develop dependence move faster, and whether this holds for other drugs, is open. The studies that bear most directly on the yes side, Randall et al. (1999) for alcohol in a treatment sample and Khan et al. (2013) for cannabis in a general-population survey, are known here only from other papers' descriptions, which disagree about the first.
debate.what_would_settle_it: A prospective cohort of young women and men followed from before first use, with use, dependence criteria and treatment recorded as they happen (repeated interviews or linked records), analysed with methods that separate the chance of ever becoming dependent from the speed of progression among those who do (for example mixture-cure or competing-risks models), with sex (including hormonal status) and gender (roles, access to treatment) measured separately; and a systematic review of telescoping studies, drug by drug, that separates treatment from general-population samples and recalled from prospectively recorded timing.

statement: In US national household surveys, women with alcohol dependence compared with men with alcohol dependence were less likely, or slower, to reach alcohol treatment in the years after their problems began, while for drug use disorders, and for treatment in the past year, no gender difference was described; treatment was uncommon for both. Some studies described by a review found that the women who did reach treatment got there sooner after first use or onset, which concerns speed among people treated, not who gets treatment. In two pooled general-population surveys (NLAES, 1991–1992, and NESARC, 2001–2002; 8,564 US-born adults aged 18 to 57 with alcohol dependence, not counting 258 first treated before dependence began; ages at onset and at first treatment recalled at a single interview), the hazard of first alcohol treatment was higher in men than in women in all five birth cohorts, significantly in people born 1954–1963 (hazard ratio 1.42, 95% CI 1.16 to 1.73) and 1964–1973 (1.55, 1.22 to 1.96), with intervals including no difference in the other three, and over all cohorts together the difference was significant (F = 22.7, p < 0.001); the models adjusted for survey, race and ethnicity, income, education, urbanicity and age at first drink, and, according to the table's footnote though not the Methods, for age; about a quarter (24.6%) of people with dependence had ever had any alcohol treatment; among people who were treated, women born 1934–1943 reached treatment sooner after dependence began (19.4 against 23.5 years) (Keyes et al., 2010). As described by a narrative review, an earlier analysis of the 1991–1992 survey (Dawson, 1996; 7,359 people with alcohol abuse or dependence; onset and treatment reported after the fact; adjustment not described) found that 23% of men and 15.1% of women had ever been treated (counting a doctor, counsellor, Alcoholics Anonymous, another professional or a treatment facility), with no gender difference in the first 8 years after onset, men 13% to 20% more likely to start treatment between 8 and 25 years after onset, and no difference among the most severely dependent; past-year alcohol treatment among people with alcohol dependence was 12.5% in women and 12.1% in men in a 1999 household survey, and gender was not associated with past-year use of substance use services in the 2002 national survey (Greenfield et al., 2007, second-hand). Women were a smaller share of people in US alcohol treatment than of people with alcohol use disorders (men to women 3.3 to 1 in treatment facilities against 2.7 to 1 in the population in 1991), and women with drinking problems more often sought help in mental-health and other non-specialist services; barriers described for women include childcare, pregnancy and fear of losing custody or of prosecution, stigma and co-occurring mental-health problems (Greenfield et al., 2007). A later review reports, from the 2015 national survey, that 10.4% of women and 11.1% of men who needed treatment for an alcohol or drug use disorder received it, that under-treatment was most marked among women with alcohol use disorder, that gender was not associated with past-year treatment use for illicit drug use disorders, and that some studies found women reached treatment sooner after first use and after onset; it adds that women with alcohol use disorder more often named stigma as a barrier in two population surveys, while other surveys found few gender differences in barriers, perhaps because they did not ask about pregnancy, childcare or family attitudes (McHugh et al., 2018, second-hand). The two analyses of the 1991–1992 survey share data and are not independent; all timing and treatment were self-reported, years later; 'treatment' was defined differently across studies; and the figures are from the USA. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated by the same team (two analyses that share a survey).
plain: Are women less likely than men to get treatment? For alcohol, somewhat. In US surveys, men with alcohol dependence reached treatment more often or sooner than women in some age groups. In one 1992 survey, as a review describes it, 23 in 100 men and 15 in 100 women with alcohol problems had ever been treated, and the gap appeared only 8 or more years after the problems began. Some studies found that the women who did get treatment got there sooner after their problems began. For drug problems, and for treatment in the past year, the reviews describe no difference. In 2015, about 10 in 100 women and 11 in 100 men who needed treatment for alcohol or drugs got it. Women more often went to mental-health services. Reviews list barriers such as childcare and fear of losing custody, but several surveys found few differences between women and men in the barriers they named, apart from stigma. People reported all of this themselves, years later, and the figures are from the US.

statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether women and men who enter treatment for alcohol or other drug use disorders differ in how long they stay or how well they do: as summarized by two narrative reviews from one research group, most large studies found no gender difference in retention, completion or outcome; where differences appeared, the 2007 review found that they generally favoured women, while most of the differences the 2018 update lists, for quitting smoking and for particular medicines, went against women; the reviews' figures are second-hand. A review of 280 articles published from 1975 to 2005 (11.8% of them randomized trials; the studies were not appraised) describes large multi-programme data sets with very few gender differences in retention (among 10,010 patients in 96 programmes, men were 20% less likely than women to stay 90 days in outpatient drug-free care; in a national study of 4,689 adults, gender was not associated with completion after adjustment), small clinical studies that disagreed (five found women more likely to drop out, two less likely), and outcome studies that mostly found no difference and, where they found one, mostly favoured women (in one study of older adults in outpatient alcohol treatment, 79.3% of women and 54% of men were abstinent at 6 months, a difference that disappeared after adjustment for length of stay, although the women still reported no heavy-drinking days in the past month against an average of four among the men) (Greenfield et al., 2007). The group's 2018 update describes no gender difference in outcome in large randomized trials (COMBINE, 1,226 people with alcohol dependence, 31% women; a prescription-opioid trial, 653 people, 40% women), none in retention across 24 NIDA Clinical Trials Network trials (more than 11,000 people), and none in completion across more than 1.7 million US treatment episodes, except that women less often completed detoxification; behavioural treatments and mutual-help groups showed no clear difference between women and men. The exceptions it lists mostly go against women: worse results in quitting smoking, nicotine replacement working better in men, and worse responses in women to disulfiram for cocaine dependence and to buspirone for cannabis and cocaine dependence (where buspirone did no better than placebo in either sex); one smoking medicine, varenicline, worked better in women in one meta-analysis and gave women more benefit than other aids in another, naltrexone findings for alcohol were mixed, and the effect of disulfiram for alcohol dependence in women is unknown because women were, for example, 1.2% of trial participants (McHugh et al., 2018). Comparisons of women-only with mixed-gender treatment were few and mixed. Of the randomized comparisons described in the 2007 review, one found no difference in early dropout, one found better retention in a women-only day programme, and in the one that compared alcohol and drug outcomes the women-only day programme did not differ from two community mixed-gender programmes and had lower abstinence than a hospital programme that cost twice as much per week; the review concludes that women may be equally well served by good programmes of either kind and that changing a programme to women-only does not by itself change outcomes (Greenfield et al., 2007). The 2018 update describes comparisons in which women in women-only programmes did better (across 43 programmes, despite greater severity; and on later crime and incarceration, designs not described), randomized trials it cites as supporting programmes designed for particular groups of women (women with children, with co-occurring psychiatric disorders or in the criminal justice system), and two trials of the group's own women's group therapy: better than mixed-gender group counselling at 6 months in a small first trial, and as effective, not more, in a larger one (McHugh et al., 2018). These comparisons are between women and men who had already entered treatment; within trials, women and men were compared as subgroups, not assigned at random; outcomes were defined in many different ways; a non-significant difference is not evidence that outcomes are the same; and several of the analyses are the reviewers' own. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: Once in treatment, do women do as well as men? Most large studies found no difference: women and men stayed in treatment about as long and had similar results. Where differences did appear, the older review found that women mostly did better, while the newer one listed more results in which women did worse, mainly in quitting smoking and with some medicines. Programmes for women only gave mixed results: in the one trial that compared results, a women-only programme showed no difference from two mixed ones and did less well than a costlier hospital programme, and some other studies favoured women-only programmes. All of this comes from two reviews by one research group, which did not check the quality of the studies, and finding no difference is not proof that results are the same.
population: Women and men who had entered treatment for alcohol or other drug use disorders, mostly in the USA, in studies described by two narrative reviews (1975–2005 and 2007–2017)
exposure: Being a woman (an observed characteristic, not assigned at random, even within trials)
comparator: Men in the same programmes or trials
outcome: Retention, completion and substance use outcomes, as each study defined them
magnitude: Second-hand, none pooled, mostly without intervals. Greenfield et al. (2007): 280 articles 1975–2005, 11.8% randomized trials; small clinical retention studies, five with more dropout in women, two with less, one mixed; 10,010 patients in 96 programmes, men 20% less likely to stay 90 days in outpatient drug-free care; 26,047 patients in 87 Los Angeles programmes, women more often completed where differences appeared; 4,689 adults (1,239 women), gender not associated with completion after adjustment; older adults, abstinence in the past 30 days at 6 months 79.3% of women vs 54% of men, not significant after adjustment for length of stay, heavy-drinking days in the past month none in women vs an average of four in men; randomized comparison of outcomes in women-only against mixed-gender day programmes, women-only no different from two community programmes, lower total abstinence than a hospital programme costing twice as much per week. McHugh et al. statement: In one pre-registered online experiment with adults who said they had no substance use or psychiatric diagnosis and knew of none in a close relative, the words used to describe a person's difficulty changed some of the attitudes readers reported, but not others, and changed what they did in a pretend money task only slightly. 1,613 adults (largest age group 18 to 25; 55.9% women; 77.1% White; recruited through university research-participation schemes, Prolific and social media; country of residence not stated) were each randomly assigned to read one short story about a person called Alex. When Alex's serious trouble at home and work was said to come from increasing drug use rather than from a health concern (819 against 741 readers), readers reported wanting more social distance from Alex (standardized difference d 0.87), saw Alex as more dangerous (d 0.78) and gave higher public-stigma scores (d 0.95; means 50.6 against 42.2): two of these differences are large by the usual standard and the third (danger) is just below it. They agreed less that the condition had genetic or disease causes (d −0.35), and their hope for Alex's recovery was the same within the study's equivalence bounds (d −0.06). In a pretend task in which readers could give or take small sums of money for Alex's answers, readers of the drug-use story took slightly more money (62.05 against 53.96 pence; d 0.14, interval 0.02 to 0.26), a difference the study could not show to be larger than its 0.20 threshold for a meaningful effect, and gave the same amount within the equivalence bounds (d −0.03). Among readers of the drug-use story, calling the condition a 'chronically relapsing brain disease' rather than a 'problem' (392 against 423) made readers agree more that it had genetic or disease causes (d 0.54; the study calls this subscale blame). With the brain-disease label, social distance (d −0.20, interval −0.36 to −0.03) and public stigma (−0.18, −0.34 to −0.02) were slightly lower, and the differences in danger (−0.11) and hope (−0.07) were smaller; all four were inconclusive, so the study could not tell whether any of them was more than trivial, and the label did not reliably change the money given or taken. Framing Alex's treatment as likely to succeed rather than uncertain (the two versions also differed in whether Alex was in a treatment programme or had seen a doctor) gave inconclusive differences on every attitude measure and on money given, and the same money taken (Pennington et al., 2023). The study measured attitudes reported after one made-up story, not how people who use drugs are actually treated by the public, health workers or services; people with a substance use or psychiatric diagnosis, or a close relative with one, could not take part; in the drug-use version four questionnaire items named opioids, so that comparison changed the questions as well as the story; the intervals printed as 99% match 98% intervals; and it did not compare person-first words with labels for the person. Kelly & Westerhoff (2010), a randomized study of two commonly used terms for people with substance-related conditions, is not yet read. Certainty: low. Status: single study.
plain: Do words about drug use change how others see a person? In one experiment, 1,613 adults online each read one short story about a person called Alex, with the wording chosen at random. When Alex's trouble was said to come from drug use rather than a health concern, readers clearly wanted to keep more distance from Alex, saw Alex as more dangerous and gave higher stigma scores. In a pretend money task they also took slightly more money from Alex, a small difference the study could not call meaningful. Calling it a 'brain disease' instead of a 'problem' made readers think more that it came from genes or illness. Readers also kept slightly less distance, but the study could not tell whether this or the label's other effects mattered. Readers rated a made-up story; people with a drug or mental health diagnosis, or a close relative with one, could not take part; and the study did not test words for the person, such as person-first words.
